reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A relatively circumscribed astrocytic tumour of children and young adults, typically superficial and involving the temporal lobe with the overlying meninges
Frequently presents with seizures owing to its cortical, temporal location
MRI commonly shows a peripheral, contrast-enhancing solid nodule with an associated cyst and, often, involvement of the adjacent leptomeninges
BRAF V600E mutation is present in a large proportion of cases and combines with CDKN2A/B deletion as a characteristic molecular signature
Histology shows pleomorphic, sometimes lipidised (xanthomatous) astrocytes, eosinophilic granular bodies and pericellular reticulin
Graded as CNS WHO grade 2 or, when mitotic activity is high (anaplastic PXA), grade 3, which behaves more aggressively
Gross total resection is the mainstay, and BRAF-targeted therapy is an option in recurrent or anaplastic BRAF V600E-mutant tumours
reference.pathophysiology: Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma is an astrocytic tumour arising superficially in the cerebral hemispheres, characteristically in the temporal lobe and often reaching the leptomeninges. It is thought to derive from astrocytes or subpial progenitor cells. Despite alarming histological pleomorphism, including large bizarre and lipid-laden cells, the typical tumour is relatively circumscribed and lower grade. Activation of the MAP kinase pathway, most often via the BRAF V600E mutation, frequently combined with homozygous deletion of CDKN2A/B, drives tumorigenesis. Higher mitotic activity defines the anaplastic (grade 3) variant, which is more prone to recurrence and progression. Its cortical position accounts for the prominence of seizures.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI to characterise the superficial nodule, cyst and meningeal involvement
Video-EEG when seizures are the presenting feature
Histopathology showing pleomorphic and xanthomatous astrocytes with eosinophilic granular bodies
BRAF V600E immunohistochemistry or molecular testing
Ki-67/MIB-1 index and mitotic count to assess for anaplastic (grade 3) features
redFlags: High mitotic activity or necrosis indicating anaplastic transformation
New focal deficits or refractory seizures
reference.prognosis: Prognosis for the grade 2 tumour is generally good after gross total resection, with prolonged survival, whereas the anaplastic (grade 3) variant recurs more readily and carries a poorer outlook. BRAF status, extent of resection and grade are the main determinants, and BRAF/MEK-directed therapy offers an option for recurrent or anaplastic BRAF V600E-mutant disease.
pitfalls: Overcalling the marked pleomorphism as glioblastoma and overtreating a lower-grade tumour
Failing to recognise anaplastic PXA and underestimating recurrence risk
Not testing for BRAF V600E, missing a targetable alteration
Incomplete resection of a superficial, potentially curable lesion
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
management: Treatment intent is curative for newly diagnosed, resectable, lower grade (CNS WHO grade 2) disease, and control or palliative leaning for anaplastic (grade 3), unresectable, or recurrent disease.

Maximal safe surgical resection is the primary and preferred treatment for newly diagnosed disease; complete resection is associated with a very favorable long term outcome, and repeat resection is a reasonable option at recurrence when a meaningful proportion of tumor can safely be removed.

A reasonable approach after gross total resection of grade 2 disease is close imaging surveillance without upfront radiotherapy, reserving radiotherapy for subtotal resection, anaplastic histology, or progression.

Adjuvant radiotherapy should be considered after subtotal resection, particularly in eloquent locations where further surgery risks significant morbidity; higher radiotherapy doses are warranted for higher grade (anaplastic) histology.

Highly conformal radiotherapy techniques are favored to limit long term CNS toxicity given the younger patient population typically affected, and stereotactic radiosurgery may be considered for limited recurrence after resection.

No optimal chemotherapy regimen is defined for this tumor group; chemotherapy is generally reserved for young children after subtotal resection with progression, or used as salvage therapy in older patients after surgery and radiotherapy have failed, with disease stabilization considered a successful outcome.

BRAF V600E mutation is a characteristic, common molecular feature of this tumor (not universal, so a wild type result does not exclude the diagnosis) and should be tested for, since it identifies candidates for BRAF-targeted therapy.

Combined BRAF inhibitor plus MEK inhibitor therapy (by drug class) is a reasonable option for BRAF V600E mutant disease that is recurrent, unresectable, or anaplastic; responses occur in a minority of patients, but responders can have durable benefit lasting more than a year, and more than two years in this specific tumor type.
Temozolomide is used with limited reported experience in this tumor group and may be considered case by case in a multidisciplinary setting, though no defined role is established.

Antiseizure medication is an important supportive care measure given the cortical, temporal location that predisposes to seizures at presentation; single agent therapy with slow dose titration is favored, with tapering considered later under specialist guidance once seizure free and off active tumor treatment.

Serial contrast enhanced brain MRI is the mainstay of surveillance after resection, to detect recurrence and identify signs of transformation to a higher grade; follow-up should be more intensive for subtotally resected or anaplastic disease and can be less frequent after gross total resection of grade 2 disease.
All patients should be managed through a neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team from diagnosis, with neurosurgical and radiation oncology input at initial diagnosis.
Re-refer promptly for radiological or clinical progression, new focal deficits, refractory seizures, or histological evidence of anaplastic transformation.
Refer to a center with access to BRAF/MEK-targeted therapy when BRAF V600E testing is positive and disease is recurrent, unresectable, or anaplastic.
